title: Study Abroad Report: Tulane University and UWA
paragraphs: My name is 中村健人, and I am a sixth-year student in the Department of Medicine of the Nagoya University School of Medicine. I was given the opportunity to study at Tulane University School of Medicine in New Orleans, in the United States, using the clinical clerkship program at overseas partner schools, and I would like to report on it. Looking back from the time I decided to study abroad to now that it is over, I am deeply moved.

The dispatch was once cancelled, but the doctors of the International Collaboration Office renegotiated, and I was able to be sent for one month. Although it was a short period, I was able to spend very fulfilling days.

In the clerkship I was allowed to rotate through pediatrics, my preferred department. In the United States pediatrics is divided into fine specialties, and in addition to general pediatrics there are pediatric nephrology, pediatric cardiology, pediatric genetics and so on, and I was assigned to pediatric hematology-oncology. While the pediatric hematology-oncology group at Nagoya University has many patients with ALL and solid tumors such as neuroblastoma, at Tulane University, because of the local character that there are many African Americans, patients with sickle cell disease made up most of them. It is also the core hospital for hemophilia in Louisiana, and because my supervising doctor specializes in bypassing agents for hemophilia with the appearance of inhibitors, I was also able to experience patients with hemophilia.

At the start of the clerkship I suffered from the language barrier, and also, because of the clerkship period, I was not given access to view the charts, so I only shadowed and had no opportunity to interact with patients. When the doctors noticed that my English was not fluent, I became like air, given no tasks, and the days passed quickly. Thinking that coming like this would be meaningless, I decided to appeal to the supervising doctor on my own. A Japanese doctor working locally also said to me, "It is different from Japan, so most things won't go well. But it is important to assert clearly what you want to do. Most of the time it doesn't work even if you assert it, but occasionally it does. Believe in that and just act." Reflecting on my attitude toward study in the clerkships in Japan, I vowed in my heart to act actively and independently from then on for the rest of the period.

By appealing in various ways, such as having the charts of outpatients printed the day before to prepare, asking for assignments, asking questions during ward rounds, and asking many times to be allowed to take histories and do physical examinations, I was gradually entrusted with more. To the doctors I must have looked like a strange Japanese who could not even speak properly, but it seems I was somehow able to make my appeal. At first I was not allowed to meet patients unless I was with a local student, but in the end I was allowed to take the history and perform the physical examination on my own, think up the assessment and plan, and present to a senior physician.

As I had been told in advance by the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, the United States is harsh toward people who cannot do things, and I was tormented by feelings of inferiority. But I think that being able to act on my own, struggling and suffering, was the greatest result I gained from this study abroad, greater than any medical knowledge I gained in the clerkship.

In the United States, no one does anything for you unless you speak up yourself, but I felt that if you act actively you get a greater response than you imagined. I think that by doing my best, however limited, the doctors' view of me gradually changed. I feel that my attitude toward learning in the clerkships in Japan was far too passive and reticent. Given this opportunity, I keenly felt the need to learn independently. I hope I can continue to study with this attitude after returning to Japan.

Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to thank Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 of the International Collaboration Office, Ms. 西尾 in charge of exchange students, the members of the pediatric hematology team at Tulane University, and my family who supported me, who gave me this valuable opportunity.

Next, I was given the opportunity to study abroad for two months at the University of Western Australia (hereafter UWA) in Perth, Australia, using the clinical clerkship program at overseas partner schools, and I would like to take this opportunity to report on it. I moved to Australia following the clinical clerkship at Tulane University in the United States, so I was able to have the very valuable experience of experiencing the medicine of two countries different from Japan.
I did my clerkship not at the UWA university hospital but at its affiliated hospitals, one month each at Fiona Stanley Hospital and Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital.

In the first month I rotated through thoracic surgery at Fiona Stanley Hospital. The clerkship began with rounds and a conference at 7 a.m., followed by observing surgery. There were two operations a day in two operating rooms, and although CABG patients made up most of them, I was able to observe a wide range, including valve replacement, lobectomy and pleurodesis for pneumothorax. I was also often allowed into the surgical field. When you enter the surgical field, the doctors fire questions at you. Listening to fast English through a mask was extremely difficult, but the doctors explained without being exasperated however many times I asked again. Before cardiac surgery started, I was taught by the anesthesiologists, was allowed to do procedures such as tracheal intubation and urinary catheterization, and was also able to receive short lectures on transesophageal echocardiography and anesthetic drugs. The doctors were kind to me, who had poor English and little medical knowledge, and at the conference on the last day of the clerkship they said, "First, an important thing, this is Kento's last day!" and took time for me to say goodbye. I was moved that they remembered me, who had been almost like air, hardly able to join the doctors' conversations (especially chit-chat).

In the second month I rotated through neurosurgery at Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital. This too began with rounds at 7 a.m., and the focus was observing surgery. There were two or three operations every day, and I was allowed into the surgical field for almost all of them. It was physically quite tough, but I think this period was the most fulfilling of my life abroad. Small operations are done by a single doctor, so as an assistant I was allowed to tie knots and suture. Here I seem to have been seen as a member of the team: they prepared a gown and gloves in my size, put my name in the operation record, and a doctor with whom I had been in surgery many times said to me, "No one is serious as much as you are." These are small things, but I was happy about them. *Grammatically it is not correct, but since it is a memorable phrase, I have included it as it is.

Throughout the clerkship I suffered from the language barrier. When the doctor explained to patients on rounds or gave mini-lectures to students, the English was clear and close to what I had practiced before going abroad, so I could catch it, but conversations among the doctors were fast English mixed with slang and abbreviations, and understanding what they were saying took great effort. Also, I often could not follow chit-chat more than medical conversation, and it was hard when everyone around was laughing and I alone did not understand. To juniors, I recommend practicing before going abroad not only the clean English of the TOEFL but also the casual English used in actual conversation. Not only in the clerkship but on days off, I think you will have many opportunities to play with local students and doctors. If your English is good enough that you understand the other person perfectly and can say what you want freely at such times, I think you can live an even more fulfilling life.

Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to thank Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 of the International Collaboration Office, Ms. 西尾 in charge of exchange students, the clinical departments that looked after me in the clerkship, and my family who supported me, who gave me this valuable opportunity.
